title: Language consistency and rejection sampling
goal:
Two pieces of the multi-stage recipe (Section 3.2.1, Equation 7; Appendix B.3.3). First, the language-consistency reward is the share of target-language words in the chain of thought: $\text{Reward}_{language} = \text{Num}(\text{Words}_{target}) / \text{Num}(\text{Words})$. Second, rejection sampling keeps only sampled responses that are correct and readable.

The paper doesn't say how it classifies a word, so this exercise uses a toy rule. Split the text on whitespace and ignore tokens that contain no letter (such as `15` or `+`). A remaining token is a target-language word when every letter in it is ASCII.

Write:

- `language_reward(cot)` returns the share of target-language words among the counted words, and `0.0` when there are none.
- `keep_response(text, gold, max_paragraph_words=60)` returns `True` when the response has the right format (the starter's `split_response` returns `None` otherwise), its answer is correct, `language_reward` of the thinking is exactly `1.0`, the thinking has no ``` code fence, and no paragraph of the thinking (blocks separated by a blank line) has more than `max_paragraph_words` words. These are the filters named in Appendix B.3.3: correct answers, no mixed languages, no long paragraphs, no code blocks.
- `rejection_sample(responses, gold, k)` returns the first `k` responses that `keep_response` accepts, in their original order.
hints: A token counts only if `any(c.isalpha() for c in token)`. A token is target-language when `all(c.isascii() for c in token if c.isalpha())`.
Split paragraphs with `think.split("\n\n")` and count `len(p.split())` for each.
`rejection_sample` must stop at `k`. Asking for more keepers than exist returns what it found.
